transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Alright thanks everyone for joining, we're gonna kick off the Optimize walkthrough today focused on quantization profiles, INT8 and FP8, quality versus latency tradeoffs. I'm Lena, AE on the account. Samir will run through the deep bits.
[00:12] Tom Reed: Hey Lena, thanks. We've got a couple folks here from ML and security. High level — clinical inference needs to be under 200ms median for some endpoints, and anything over 400ms is not acceptable for user-facing flows.
[00:25] Karen Liu: Yeah we also care about prediction fidelity, even small hallucinations are problematic. We'll need to see quality metrics, and the security folks want to validate KMS and VPC.
[00:36] Lena Park: Totally, we'll cover profiling methodology and sample metrics. Samir?
[00:40] Samir Patel: Cool, thanks. So quick agenda: explain the difference between INT8 and FP8, show tradeoffs, then an example of how Redwood Optimize generates a quant profile and recommends a hybrid approach.
[00:50] Samir Patel: So INT8 reduces model memory and inference compute by roughly 2-4x depending on kernel and hardware, it's been the go-to for cost-savings. FP8 is newer — it tends to preserve dynamic range better for some layers and can give less quality regression for certain LLMs. In our experience FP8 can give similar memory wins to INT8 with fewer quality blips in generation tasks, but that depends a lot on model architecture and prompt distribution.
[01:20] Rajesh Iyer: Quick question — are these numbers on A100 or cheaper GPUs? Our Dedicated plan would likely run on A10s.
[01:26] Samir Patel: Great question. The examples I'm going to show are on A10-like instances; we also have A100 runs in appendix. On A10 we saw INT8 latency improvements ~25-35% p50 and FP8 ~20-30% but with slightly better quality retention for FP8 on some benchmarks.
[01:45] Karen Liu: How do you quantify quality? We need deterministic metrics, not just human eyeballs.
[01:50] Samir Patel: We use a mix — automated similarity metrics (BLEU/ROUGE-ish proxies depending on task) plus our eval harness that runs scenario-specific prompts and checks for semantic correctness and hallucination counts. For the benchmark we recommend a labeled prompt set you provide — e.g., 500 clinical QA prompts — and we compute delta against float32 baseline.
[02:12] Maya Gonzales: From security, how do you handle model artifacts and keys? If we bring Redwood Private, is KMS on our side?
[02:19] Lena Park: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM, you manage keys. For Dedicated/Hosted we offer envelope encryption and can integrate with your cloud KMS. We'll share the security packet after — SOC2, diagram of where keys live, audit log samples.
[02:36] Samir Patel: Back to quantization: one practical approach is hybrid quantization — keep critical layers or attention weights in FP16 while quantizing feed-forward or other layers to INT8/FP8. That tends to preserve quality while getting most of the performance benefits. Redwood Optimize can generate candidate profiles and then run a short eval sweep to recommend the best safe profile.
[02:58] Tom Reed: What's the typical turnaround to go from profile generation to validated recommendation?
[03:02] Samir Patel: Usually a couple of hours for the profile generation on a representative checkpoint, then a couple days of eval depending on the size of your eval set. For our quick POC we do a 3-day run — profile, smoke tests, and a small quality pass.
[03:17] Karen Liu: Are there any cases where INT8 is strictly better than FP8 or vice versa?
[03:21] Samir Patel: Depends on model family. For decoder-only models trained with lower numeric sensitivity INT8 often works great. For some larger mixed-precision models FP8 preserves rare-token generation better. Also the compiler/runtime kernels matter — some HW provide faster INT8 paths. We surface those kernel/throughput tradeoffs in the Optimize UI.
[03:42] [00:04:00] Speaker 1: Sorry interjection, we ran a small internal test and saw some samples where INT8 introduced odd tokenization errors — like generating slightly off medical abbreviations.
[03:53] Samir Patel: Good point, that's why we recommend the hybrid approach for safety-sensitive tokens. We can pin those tokens or preserve their embedding/attention layers in higher precision.
[04:07] Rajesh Iyer: On the infra side, does Redwood support rolling rollouts? If we see a regression in production we want automatic fallback.
[04:13] Lena Park: Yes — rollouts, canarying, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies are supported. You can configure per-route policies in the Console and set SLO triggers. If a quantized variant regresses above a threshold, traffic automatically falls back to a baseline model.
[04:27] Samir Patel: Also worth noting: KV cache and prefix caching interact with quantization; sometimes cold-starts show different latency. Our runtime handles KV cache quant conversions so warm cache behavior is consistent.
[04:40] Karen Liu: Latency numbers we need — can you summarize p50/p95 improvements and token throughput for A10?
[04:45] Samir Patel: Sure — rough numbers from internal runs on an A10: float32 baseline p50 token latency ~18ms/token, INT8 ~12-14ms/token (25-33% reduction), FP8 ~13-15ms/token (roughly 20-28% reduction). p95 gaps are smaller but still material. In batching scenarios throughput increases similarly; INT8 often gives best throughput but FP8 wins on quality-sensitive seqs. Those are ballpark; we'll run Beacon's prompts to get precise numbers.
[05:16] Tom Reed: For clinical UI flows median under 200ms is our requirement. If we pick a 4-8 token response typical what does that mean?
[05:24] Samir Patel: If you have a 6-token average and p50 per-token 14ms, that's under 100ms p50 excluding network. With network and app overhead you should be comfortably under 200ms. We'll account for your network egress and region in the POC.
[05:42] Karen Liu: Any impact on hallucination frequency with FP8 vs INT8?
[05:47] Samir Patel: In our evals FP8 tends to have slightly fewer hallucinations for rare-slot generation — but again it's model and prompt dependent. That's why the POC and labeled eval set are key.
[05:58] [00:06:00] Speaker 2: Are you able to quantize on non-trainable checkpoints? We can't provide training pipelines.
[06:04] Samir Patel: Yes, quantization profiles are generated offline and applied to the saved checkpoint — no retraining needed. For edge cases where quantization fails we recommend small calibration runs; we don't require full retrain.
[06:18] Rajesh Iyer: What about monitoring — can we get per-route token-level cost and quality dashboards?
[06:23] Lena Park: Absolutely, Redwood Console shows token-level cost, latency by model/route, and integrates eval regressions into Canary dashboards so you can track quality and cost simultaneously.
[06:33] Maya Gonzales: For audit purposes we need immutable logs of model versions and which quant profile was used for a request.
[06:38] Samir Patel: We store model/version/profile metadata with each request trace; you can export that for audits. For Private deployments the logs can be routed to your SIEM.
[06:49] Karen Liu: On billing, roughly how much do we save if INT8 reduces token computation 30%?
[06:55] Lena Park: Cost savings translate but depend on your pricing plan. For Hosted plans you typically see 20-40% cost reduction on compute line items. For Dedicated it reduces GPU hours used — we'll give an estimate after we run your sample workload.
[07:07] Tom Reed: Okay good. What's the proposed POC scope?
[07:10] Samir Patel: We propose: 1) you provide 500 de-identified prompts and target metrics; 2) Redwood runs INT8/FP8 profile generation and a 3-day benchmark on representative hardware; 3) we provide a report with p50/p95 latency, throughput, and quality deltas vs float32 plus recommended safe profile.
[07:26] Karen Liu: That sounds reasonable.
[07:28] Lena Park: Great. We'll also share the benchmark template and security packet. Any other risks or blockers?
[07:34] Maya Gonzales: Just one — we need to confirm data residency requirements for any hosted trial. If data can't leave the region, we'll need a Private or Dedicated trial in our cloud region.
[07:45] Lena Park: Noted — we'll include region-specific options and flag Dedicated/Private paths.
[07:50] Samir Patel: Quick note on hybrid profiles — we can mark attention weight matrices and token embeddings to stay FP16 and quantize the rest; in many cases that gets you 80-90% of the perf wins with minimal quality delta.
[08:06] Rajesh Iyer: How do we validate token-level preservation for critical abbreviations?
[08:10] Samir Patel: You can include those tokens in a small protected token set; Optimize will preserve their embeddings or treat them as pinned and not quantize that subset. We'll show how to configure that in the Console.
[08:22] [00:08:30] Speaker 3: minor note — the transcription here might say "FP8" as "F P eight" sometimes in our export, ignore that.
[08:29] Lena Park: Good call. Any final questions?
[08:31] Tom Reed: No. Let's run the POC. I'll coordinate with Rajesh and Maya to deliver the sample set.
[08:36] Lena Park: Perfect. We'll follow up with the docs and proposed start date. Thanks everyone.
[08:42] [END]
